basis: Independently curated original deck retained in full, with original note-based additions reviewed against the subject specification. External notes supply coverage prompts, not verbatim cards.

base_cards.front: What does HDI stand for?
back: Human Development Index.

base_cards.front: What is urbanisation?
back: An increase in the proportion of people living in urban areas.

base_cards.front: How many people must a city have to be called a megacity?
back: More than 10 million.

base_cards.front: Name Ethiopia's major export crop.
back: Coffee.

base_cards.front: On which river is Rosario located?
back: The Paraná River.

base_cards.front: Name the goat-sharing system used in the Oxfam project.
back: Hirbaa-dabaree.

base_cards.front: Give two components of HDI.
back: Life expectancy.
Education or income per person.

base_cards.front: Explain one limitation of GNI per person.
back: It is a national average.
It can hide large differences between rich and poor people.

base_cards.front: Give one push and one pull factor for rural-to-urban migration.
back: Push: few rural jobs or drought.
Pull: urban employment, education or healthcare.

base_cards.front: Give two reasons why Ethiopia's development is difficult.
back: It is landlocked, increasing trade costs.
Drought, conflict, debt or weak infrastructure restrict progress.

base_cards.front: Explain how goat aid can create an income.
back: Goats reproduce and create a growing asset.
Families can sell offspring or goat products.

base_cards.front: Give two important economic roles of Rosario.
back: Paraná River port and export centre.
Food processing, manufacturing, logistics or regional services.

base_cards.front: Explain how colonialism can continue to affect development.
back: Colonial economies often focused on exporting raw materials.
Infrastructure linked resources to ports rather than joining communities.
Dependence on low-value exports may therefore continue after independence.

base_cards.front: Explain how foreign direct investment may support Ethiopia's development.
back: Foreign firms may build factories and infrastructure.
They create jobs, training, exports and tax income.
These benefits can raise incomes and fund services if they remain in Ethiopia.

base_cards.front: Explain why rapid urban growth may cause informal settlements.
back: Migration and natural increase raise housing demand quickly.
Formal homes may be too few or too expensive.
Lower-income families build on unplanned land without full services.

base_cards.front: Explain one way Rosario's urban agriculture programme is sustainable.
back: Unused urban land is turned into productive gardens.
Local growers earn income and supply nearby food.
Shorter supply chains and extra green space can reduce environmental pressure.

base_cards.front: Explain one advantage and one limitation of using HDI.
back: Advantage: it combines health, education and income, so it is broader than a single economic measure.
Limitation: it is still a national average, so regional and social inequalities may be hidden.

base_cards.front: Explain two ways rapid urbanisation can benefit a city.
back: A larger labour force attracts firms and supports business growth.
A bigger population creates demand that can justify better transport, education and healthcare.

base_cards.front: Explain two limitations of the Oxfam goat-aid project.
back: Goats remain vulnerable to severe drought, disease and shortage of grazing or water.
A small livestock project cannot by itself solve poor infrastructure, education or healthcare.

base_cards.front: Explain how Rosario Hábitat improved informal settlements.
back: It combined secure land ownership and basic infrastructure with community participation.
Employment support and selective relocation addressed social needs as well as the physical condition of housing.

additions.front: Which three dimensions make up HDI?
back: Health, measured by life expectancy; education, measured by schooling; and income, measured using GNI per person.

additions.front: Does HDI directly measure inequality?
back: No. It combines national averages, which can conceal differences between regions and social groups.

additions.front: Why use purchasing-power-adjusted income?
back: The same amount of money buys different quantities in different countries. The adjustment makes comparisons of living standards more meaningful.

additions.front: Why is high national income insufficient evidence of good living conditions for everyone?
back: It is an average. A small wealthy group can raise it while many households lack affordable services.

additions.front: How can dependence on one agricultural export make development vulnerable?
back: Drought can reduce output and changing world prices can reduce earnings. Less income is then available for households and public investment.

additions.front: Does a landlocked country have no overseas trade?
back: No. It can use neighbouring countries’ ports, although distance, border procedures and disruption can raise costs.

additions.front: How can limited education reinforce poverty?
back: It can restrict skills and job opportunities, keeping incomes low and making further education or healthcare harder to afford.

additions.front: How do emergency and development aid differ?
back: Emergency aid meets urgent crisis needs. Development aid supports longer-term improvements, such as skills, infrastructure or livelihoods.

additions.front: What distinguishes bilateral from multilateral aid?
back: Bilateral aid comes from one government to another country. Multilateral aid is channelled through an international organisation supported by several countries.

additions.front: What is tied aid?
back: Aid with conditions attached, such as requiring purchases from the donor country. Those conditions may reduce the recipient’s choice.

additions.front: Why can a grant and a loan have different long-term effects?
back: A grant does not need repayment. A loan must be repaid, so future debt servicing may compete with spending on services.

additions.front: What makes a project bottom-up?
back: Local people help identify needs and make decisions, rather than only receiving a plan designed elsewhere.

additions.front: What are Rostow’s five stages, in order?
back: Traditional society; preconditions for take-off; take-off; drive to maturity; high mass consumption.

additions.front: Why should Ethiopia not simply be labelled as one fixed Rostow stage?
back: Its regions and sectors change unevenly. Infrastructure and industry show some take-off features while many livelihoods remain agricultural.

additions.front: What is the main limitation of Rostow’s suggested path?
back: It assumes a broadly Western route and underplays unequal external relationships, conflict, inequality and environmental limits.

additions.front: How does urbanisation differ from urban growth?
back: Urbanisation is a rise in the proportion living in urban areas. Urban growth is an increase in the number living there.

additions.front: Must a world city also be a megacity?
back: No. World-city status concerns international influence; megacity status concerns a population over 10 million.

additions.front: Why can urban natural increase occur without urbanisation?
back: Births can raise urban numbers while the rural population also grows. The urban proportion need not increase.

additions.front: Why might rural-to-urban migrants not obtain the opportunities they expect?
back: Demand for secure jobs and affordable housing may exceed supply, leaving some migrants in insecure employment or poorly serviced housing.

additions.front: Is every self-employed worker in the informal economy?
back: No. A self-employed business can be registered and regulated. Informality concerns operation outside formal arrangements.

additions.front: Why did the Kanbi goat project pass offspring between households?
back: It spread benefits through the traditional hirbaa-dabaree sharing system, extending livelihoods without buying a whole new herd for every family.

additions.front: Why does Rosario Hábitat combine services and tenure with housing?
back: A house alone does not provide sanitation, drainage, secure ownership or employment opportunities. The linked measures address several causes of poor living conditions.
